Why is that the policy we should follow?

It seemed like a good starting point considering we're a Linux Foundation project.  If we want to deviate, I'm open to it.  Do you want me to put that in the commit message or was there a specific deviation you wanted?
nvm on the 2nd question.  Sounds you want the specific model requirements removed.   At a minimum I can move those to another patch.

I would suggest we also reference the LF statement on generative code:

https://www.linuxfoundation.org/legal/generative-ai

NIT: May be good to add a clear statement that contributors are responsible for licensing compliance in AI‑assisted contributions.
I think that's covered in the next section?  Is there something else we should add?
Do we have to add Assisted-by for every AI suggestion? Like Minor use of AI tools also required this?
What are we trying to accomplish by this section?  I get that Linux did it but what do we have to gain by having this?  What do we have to lose?

This came because I'm personally reviewing a lot of patches with AI hallucinations and it's taking considerable time.  Having an attribution would allow me to prioritize appropriately, and know when I'm dealing with an LLM versus a human, and review accordingly.
I think so.  It's a pretty minor thing.
OpenBMC
Done

In place of "should" I'd prefer "can". A lot of new tools, like IBM Bob, utilize dynamic models based on the query so it's not possible to know which model is used for each assist. Also, I just think in general adding this Assited-by should be optional.

💯 .  

I'll elaborate why in another comment but I would not be in favor of any AI attribution, but I would be strongly opposed to "must" or "should" language.  There are multiple cases in my own flow at the top of mind where I could not specify this properly.

1. I usually use opencode as my "AI agent".  While I have a few models that I typically default to, I don't really want to keep track of which model I used for a particular commit.  I may switch between models in the course of creating a commit (or commit series).  Also, opencode will sometimes "fall back" to different models when it gets an error from the API endpoints.

2. Meta, having their own foundational LLM model development, has internal models that I can use for OpenBMC development which may be unreleased and/or unannounced.  I would not be able to reference the model being used and even if I were able to it would have to be an internal codename which is probably not useful.

Beyond that, how are we going to know if someone doesn't specify?  Are we going to start using an LLM-grader like colleges have to _detect_ [potentially] generated code?

Andrew, ack on "can".

Patrick, how are you handling that for kernel contributions then if your AI models are private?  I care a lot less about the specific model used.  In the above case, I'd assume "opencode" would just be your agent name?

Why does "knowing" matter in the context of this?  We can assume good intent from people submitting.  This isn't meant to be a police action, it's intended to know that when we see a hallucination, or something that doesn't make sense, we can add the appropriate pointers so that those AIs can generate the correct code the first time.

> how are you handling that for kernel contributions then if your AI models are private? 

I don't do much kernel development and I haven't seen any internal discussion on this.  I can start it.

> I'd assume "opencode" would just be your agent name?

The kernel seems all over the place.  Most show "Claude:claude-...".  I don't even know what "Claude" refers to in this case because I image most kernel developers are using `claude-cli` if they referenced `Claude` here.

https://gist.github.com/williamspatrick/597965579f12eb7695a923407d41e1d2

I guess "unknown" or "unnamed" is an option that some of the kernel patches use for the "I'm not going to tell you what I'm using" option.  I guess I can just add `Assisted-by: unnamed:unnamed` to all my commits.  😄

That's fine if it's truly secret, and it's not my intent to force you to publish your internal models, but knowing you used a model helps.  What I really want to know is when I'm trying to review a security conscious patch, was this generated by an LLM with a limited context, or was it generated by an LLM that the submitter didn't review.  We had a case recently in bmcweb where two different patches hallucinated essentially the same openssl code.  It would've been good to know that a model was used, and if they were using the same model so we can add guidance in documentation for the models to find.

As far as the kernel being all over the place, I'm assuming this doc is the response to them being all over the place?  It was only recently merged.

If the "should" statement is a sticking point, I can remove it to try to get some consensus.  Let me know what your kernel people say.

I don't think that knowing the AI model is beneficial to us other than "what are people using that they've found success with".  I do think that it adds risk to the project.  For that reason I would not be in favor of anything strong than "can" and I would rather it is not encouraged.

While we have said on line 22 that the human submitter is "responsible for ensuring compliance with licensing requirements" and "taking full responsibility for the contribution" practically speaking nobody (even the best copyright lawyers) cannot say what the final copyright implications are of LLM generated code yet because it really hasn't gone through any court cases.  Every contributor is just going to say "yeah, yeah, whatever ... this works and I'm going to submit it".

LF makes this statement in their [LLM policy]:

> Some tools provide features that can assist contributors. For example, some tools provide a feature that suppresses responses that are similar  to third party materials in the AI tool’s output, or a feature that flags similarity between copyrighted training data or other materials owned by third parties and the AI tool’s output and provides information about the licensing terms that apply to such third party materials. 

The implication of that is effectively: "some tools and/or models might be generating code that is too similar to training data and might be ruled as a copyright violation in the future".  If a few years from now there are court cases around this, we may find that company X or tool A did it "right" while company Y or tool B did it "wrong" in terms of how the training and/or generation lines up with legal precedent.

By putting the Assisted-by tag in here we make it far easier for someone to say "you were using a 'bad' tool and I'm going to assert copyright violations" or for some of the participants of the project here to deem there is too much legal risk because too many of our commits used a "bad bad" (unless we go through a huge effort to rewrite all code that we generated by _Bad Model_.  If we leave this out we put the onus on the IP owners to find and assert so-called violations (and we make it harder on them to find and filter).

[LLM policy]: https://www.linuxfoundation.org/legal/generative-ai

Overall I'm not against the above, but would like to understand why the kernel seems to have a different policy here than what's on the LF website.  Do you know?

> Do you know how the kernel overcame this?

There was literally zero discussion of this patch on the mailing list, so honestly, I have no idea.  I don't really even see any "higher ups" having weighed in on it.

https://lore.kernel.org/lkml/20251223122110.2496946-1-sashal@kernel.org/

There was the LWN article where I guess a lot of this discussion happened at the Maintainers Summit last year.  https://lwn.net/Articles/1049830/

From the article there was discussion and concerns about the same copyright issues I have.  A few snippets:

> Ted Ts'o said ...we do not worry about that problem now, he said, and it has almost never actually come up.

> Dave Airlie ... said, any copyrighted code put into a patch by an LLM is likely to have come from the kernel itself.

1) The kernel doesn't really worry about clean-up from DCO violations.
2) They believe the kernel is a unique enough environment that there probably isn't tons of training material that wasn't actually already the kernel.

On (1), I don't know if us being a smaller project is better or worse in this regard.  On (2), that's probably less true for us.

At the end of the article it seems like they are non-enforcing this as well:

> As the session moved toward a close, Levin said he would post a documentation patch asking LLM tools to add an Assisted-by tag, but would not make an effort to enforce the rule. There was some final discussion on the details of that tag, which seems sure to evolve over time.
That's good background.  Agreed we're likely more subject to copyright.  Where we started was that this said "should", which I think is non enforcing as well?
